title: Coloring A Border
statement:
`grid` is an `m x n` matrix in which every value is the color of that cell. Cells are **adjacent** when they share a side (up, down, left or right). A **connected component** is a maximal group of cells of one color in which you can walk from any cell to any other by steps between adjacent cells of that color.

Take the component that contains `grid[row][col]`. A cell of that component is on its **border** if it lies in the first or last row or column of the grid, or if at least one adjacent cell is not part of the component. Paint every border cell with `color`, leave all other cells unchanged, and return the resulting grid. Whether a cell is on the border is decided by the original colors, before any painting.
signature: int[][] colorBorder(int[][] grid, int row, int col, int color)
notes:
## Intuition

First find the whole component with a flood fill from `(row, col)`, stepping only onto neighbours of the same original color. While visiting a cell we can already tell whether it is on the border: one of its four neighbours is off the grid or has a different color. The catch is timing. If we painted border cells during the search, a later cell next to a freshly painted one would think that neighbour is outside the component. So the search only **collects** border cells, and painting happens afterwards.

## Approach

1. Remember `original = grid[row][col]` and mark the start as `seen`; push it on `stack`.
2. Pop a cell `(r, c)` and look at its four neighbours `(nr, nc)`.
3. A neighbour that is off the grid or not `original` makes this cell a border cell (`onBorder = true`).
4. A neighbour of the same color that is not yet `seen` belongs to the component: mark it and push it.
5. After the four checks, add `(r, c)` to `border` if `onBorder` is set.
6. When the stack is empty, paint every cell in `border` with `color` and return `grid`.

## Example 1, step by step

`grid = [[1,1],[1,2]]`, start `(0,0)`, `original = 1`. Popping `(0,0)`: up and left are off the grid, so it is a border cell; `(1,0)` and `(0,1)` are pushed. `(0,1)` touches the grid edge and the `2` below it; `(1,0)` touches the edge and the `2` to its right. All three are border cells, so painting them with 3 gives `[[3,3],[3,2]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m·n): each cell is pushed at most once and checks four neighbours.
- Space: O(m·n) for `seen`, `stack` and `border`.

## Pitfalls

- Painting during the search changes colors that later border checks read; collect first, paint last.
- `color` may equal the original color. Using "already painted" as the visited mark then loops forever; a separate `seen` grid avoids that.
- A cell on the outer edge of the grid is a border cell even when all its in-grid neighbours are in the component.
- Only side neighbours count; diagonal cells of the same color are not connected.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rows`, `cols` | the grid's dimensions |
| `original` | the color of the starting component |
| `seen` | which cells have already been added to the search |
| `stack` | component cells waiting to be examined |
| `border` | component cells that must be painted |
| `r`, `c` / `nr`, `nc` | the current cell and one of its neighbours |
| `onBorder` | whether the current cell touches the edge or another color |
